newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Singapore's top public flats promise new luxuries.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Singapore's top public flats promise new luxuries.

text.p: In fast-growing Singapore, the government is promoting an affordable and highly sought after status symbol -- public executive condominiums.
The new top-of-the-line, government-subsidised flats have the same standards as private condominiums, including marble floors, 50-metre swimming pools and in some cases clubhouses and putting greens.
But they are more affordable.
Analysts say a steady supply of executive condominiums also helps restrain lofty private property prices by limiting demand for more expensive apartments.

In a country where 86 percent of people live in high-rise government flats, and 90 percent of dwellers own them, authorities feel it is crucial to keep up to date with rising incomes and changing lifestyles.
Industry experts said public executive condominiums will help meet rising aspirations in the city state, where annual per-capita income has surpassed US$24,000.
Unlike some public housing schemes in other countries, Singaporeans can buy their units -- under certain conditions.

The government offers the apartments below market prices through subsidised land sales, but buyers must meet strict home ownership standards, such as income limits, to qualify for the new range of executive condominiums.
Public housing at the high-end is now designed and built by private architects and developers, giving such units a more creative appearance compared with older block-designed flats.

"It may be a shade inferior on finishes, but only a shade. The restriction is on whether I am entitled to buy, and on resale," Tan Tiong Cheng, managing director of Knight Frank said, referring to a series of rules governing ownership.

"Executive condominiums are an answer to the sandwich class, those who don't fit public housing but find private housing too expensive," Tan said. He said apartments in such complexes represented good value at S$410 ($290) per square feet.
A private condominium, with no controls on ownership, costs about 30 percent more.
KEEPING THE LID ON RISING PROPERTY PRICES
Executive condominiums have also helped dampen Singapore's recent property boom, proving a negative for sellers.
"It's caused downward pressure on property prices. It's definitely bad news for private developers," Lim Chung Chun, an investment analyst for ING Barings, said.
The government's annual target for about 4,000 subsidised condominium apartments will reduce demand for private complexes, he said.
Public housing affordability has always been a prominent feature in the city-state.
In recent elections, voters returned the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) to power in a landslide victory and a hotly debated issue was who would be eligible for public housing renovations.
Critics said fears that public flats would deteriorate prompted many to support Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and PAP candidates on January 2.
Goh had told voters if they voted for the opposition, they would be last in line for lucrative upgrading projects.

"Then you'll be left behind. Then in 20, 30 years' time, the whole of Singapore will be bustling away and your estate, through your own choice, will be left behind. They become slums. That's my message," Goh said.
Singapore's public housing estates have been enhanced by upgrading, and values have risen as a result.
"Executive condos are equivalent of a fairly standard range condominium," a spokesman for NTUC Choice Homes, a developer for the latest executive condominium Simei Green, told Reuters.
Unlike previous types of public housing, these units come with parquet and marble floors, kitchen amenities, a 50-metre swimming pool, tennis courts, putting green and clubhouse.
The Simei apartments range in price from Singapore $366,000 ($261,000) to $642,000 ($459,000).
At a recent sale, eight people applied for each of the 602 apartments for sale in one complex.
SOME CONCESSIONS FOR THE DISCOUNT
Executive condominiums allow families to upgrade from five-room executive apartments, and help reduce the price gap between public and private housing.
The concession, however, is that buyers who sell their flats within five years have to pay a penalty.
After five years they may only resell to a Singapore citizen or permanent resident. The flat becomes a full-fledged private facility only after 10 years.
Another catch is that a family's gross monthly income must not exceed Singapore $10,000 (US$7,140).

Commenting on the demand for these condominiums compared with their price, chairman of NTUC Choice Homes Ng Ser Miang said, "(it) has a clear objective to act as a moderating force in the housing market."
In any case, experts feel executive condominiums will be a growing trend in public housing as income and expectations improve in the next decade.
